title: Teaching modifications and injury boundaries
audience: Yoga and Pilates instructors who teach modifications, respond to injury, and decide when to refer a student to a health professional
learningOutcomes: Offer a modification for a posture without diagnosing the student's condition
Identify the injury signs that require the class to stop and the student to be referred
Explain why a yoga or Pilates certificate is not a clinical or therapeutic authority, and how that applies to hands-on adjustments
referencesAtStart: No legal or regulatory claim is relied on in this lesson. The licence, hands-on adjustment and AusActive points are marked SECONDARY.

instruction.heading: Modifications: offer options, do not diagnose
instruction.body: A modification is a change to a posture that makes it suitable for a student, for example a lower position, a support, or a shorter hold. The instructor offers modifications from the start of the class, so that a student who is unsure can choose one without explaining why. The instructor must not diagnose the student's condition, must not name an injury, and must not tell the student that a pain is nothing. Describe what you can see and offer an option. Where a student describes an injury or an ongoing condition, the instructor records it as the student describes it, and refers the student to a medical practitioner or allied health professional for advice before the student attempts any posture that aggravates the condition. The business's modification and referral procedure is held in {{business:procedures.approved_sop}}.

instruction.heading: Injury boundaries and when the class must stop
instruction.body: The class must stop for an individual where a student reports sharp pain, numbness, dizziness, chest tightness, breathlessness out of proportion to effort, or any sudden injury. The instructor must keep the student safe, avoid moving the student further, and advise medical attention where the symptoms are serious. The screening approach in “Client screening and health-questionnaire boundaries” applies to yoga and Pilates as well. Where a student has an injury that a health professional has told them to avoid a posture for, the instructor must respect that advice and must not coach the posture through pain.

instruction.heading: Hands-on adjustments and the limits of a certificate
instruction.body: Hands-on adjustments, where an instructor touches a student to guide a posture, carry risk. They need the student's clear consent, a clear reason, and training in the technique. The business should not make hands-on adjustments unless it has the training and the student's consent recorded. A teaching certificate is a qualification, not a clinical or therapeutic authority. It does not allow the instructor to diagnose, treat or advise on a medical condition. Completing this lesson does not give any of those authorities.

procedure: Offer modifications at the start of the class, and make clear that a student can choose one without explanation
When a student describes an injury or a condition, record it as described, and refer the student to a medical practitioner or allied health professional before the posture is attempted
Stop the class for an individual at any sign of sharp pain, numbness, dizziness, chest tightness or breathlessness, and keep the student safe
Respect any posture restriction a health professional has given, and do not coach the student through pain
Use hands-on adjustment only with the student's consent and training, and record each instance where the business policy requires it
Record each injury report, referral and stop, with the date and the action taken

workedExamples.situation: A student tells the instructor she has had a knee operation and her physiotherapist has told her to avoid deep squats. The class is about to do a deep squat sequence.
workedExamples.reasoning: The physiotherapist's restriction is the guide, so the instructor should not coach the student into a deep squat. The instructor should offer a modification, such as a supported position or a shallower range, and should not diagnose the knee. The restriction should be recorded. The instructor should not ask the student to push through pain.

workedExamples.situation: A student in a Pilates class becomes pale, says her chest feels tight, and then becomes dizzy when she sits up.
workedExamples.reasoning: Chest tightness and dizziness are stop signs. The instructor stops the student, keeps her safe in a seated or lying position, advises urgent medical attention if the symptoms continue or are serious, and records the incident. The instructor does not decide the cause and does not resume the class for that student. The class continues for the other students only if the instructor can supervise them safely.

equipmentAndPpe: Props for modifications, such as blocks, bolsters and straps
First-aid kit and phone with the emergency contact list

commonErrors.error: Naming an injury or telling a student that a pain is nothing.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe what you see, offer a modification, and refer the student to a health professional.

commonErrors.error: Coaching a student through pain to keep the class moving.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop the posture for that student and offer a modification or rest.

commonErrors.error: Making hands-on adjustments without consent or training.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not adjust a student by hand unless the training and the student's consent are recorded.

commonErrors.error: Stating that a teaching certificate allows the instructor to advise on a condition.
commonErrors.prevention: A certificate is a teaching qualification. It gives no clinical or therapeutic authority.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: No state licence for yoga or Pilates instructors was found in the sources checked for Victoria.
The AusActive pre-exercise screening tool is industry guidance from a non-official body, SECONDARY, with no confirmed legal status.
The rules for hands-on adjustments were not researched.
A teaching qualification does not grant a clinical, diagnostic or therapeutic authority. This lesson does not grant one.

qualityStandard: Modifications are offered at the start of every class
Every injury report is recorded as described, with the referral made
Every stop for a student is recorded with the action taken
No hands-on adjustment is made without consent and training
documentationEvidence: Injury report and referral record for each student who reports a condition
Stop record for each class stopped for a student
Consent and training record for hands-on adjustments, where used
Restriction record for any posture restriction given by a health professional
summary: Offer modifications; do not diagnose or name an injury
Stop for warning signs, keep the student safe and refer
Hands-on adjustment needs consent and training.
Completing this lesson does not give clinical or therapeutic authority

knowledgeChecks.question: A student says her physiotherapist has told her to avoid deep squats. What should the instructor do?
options: Offer a modification and record the restriction, without coaching through pain
Coach the deep squat, since the class is about to do it now with the group
Ask the student to push through and see how it feels to them today

knowledgeChecks.question: A student feels chest tightness and dizziness during a class. What is the correct action?
options: Continue the class, since the student may be fine after the moment and the brief pause at the mat
Stop the student, keep them safe, advise urgent medical attention if serious, and record the incident
Ask the student to lie down and resume the whole class in ten minutes or so with the group

knowledgeChecks.question: What is a teaching certificate, according to the lesson?
options: A qualification, not a clinical or therapeutic authority
A permit to treat back pain
